---
title: "Two Rankings from One Posterior: A Bayesian Power Rating and a Wins-Above-Benchmark Resume for College Football"
abstract: "A college football ranking is asked to answer two different questions: which team is better, and which team has earned more. The first is predictive and should use every informative signal, including margin of victory; the second is retrodictive and should reward only results. We answer both from a single Bayesian model. Team strength is a latent quantity in points on a neutral field, observed through two per-game signals, the opponent-free efficiency margin measured by expected points added and the regulation scoreboard margin, with the margin modelled conditionally on the efficiency residual so that the two are not counted as independent evidence. Strength is pooled within conferences and within three divisional tiers and carried over between seasons by an estimated coefficient. The power rating is the posterior of strength. The resume is Wins Above Benchmark: the number of wins a team has beyond what the twelfth-best team would be expected to win against the same schedule at the same venues, computed per posterior draw so that the benchmark, the opponents and the resulting ranks all carry their uncertainty. We show that under a Gaussian version of the model the efficiency signal adds only a few percent of per-game Fisher information about strength once the margin is observed, prove the elementary properties that make Wins Above Benchmark a sensible resume measure, and evaluate the model on every week of every season from 2014 to the present: every weekly posterior checked against convergence gates, and a rolling out-of-sample backtest of every game scored against results and closing betting lines."

```{r, data}
bt <- tr("backtest")

checks <- Filter(Negate(is.null), tr("checks"))

pooled <- read.csv(file.path(root, "analysis/structural_pooled.csv"))

seasons <- sort(unique(params$season))
first_season <- min(seasons)
current <- max(seasons)
# A season is complete once its postseason snapshot exists.
complete <- sort(unique(params$season[params$week_label == "Postseason"]))
last_full <- max(complete)

final <- params |> group_by(season) |> filter(week == max(week)) |> ungroup()
final_full <- final |> filter(season %in% complete)

n_snap <- nrow(params)
n_pass <- sum(params$passed)
n_retry <- sum(params$attempts > 1)
n_games_all <- sum(games$completed, na.rm = TRUE)

ov <- bt$overall
bt_all <- ov |> filter(scope == "All games")
bt_fbs <- ov |> filter(scope == "FBS vs FBS")
bt_late <- ov |> filter(scope == "FBS vs FBS, week 5+")

# The Gaussian information calculation of @sec-info, at each complete season's
# final posterior mean.
info <- final_full |>
  transmute(
    season, lambda, kappa, sigma_eff, sigma_m, nu,
    S11 = sigma_eff^2, S12 = kappa * sigma_eff^2, S22 = sigma_m^2 + kappa^2 * sigma_eff^2,
    i_y = 1 / S22,
    i_joint = lambda^2 / sigma_eff^2 + (1 - kappa * lambda)^2 / sigma_m^2,
    gain = i_joint / i_y - 1,
    lambda_star = S12 / S22,
    r2 = kappa^2 * sigma_eff^2 / S22
  )

fin_last <- ratings |> filter(season == last_full, week == max(week), tier == 1)
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Every autumn, some one hundred and thirty teams in the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) play about twelve games each, against opponents they largely do not choose, and at the end a committee selects twelve of them for a playoff. The schedule graph is sparse: a team plays fewer than a tenth of the other teams in its division, most of them from its own conference, and conferences are linked by a few dozen non-conference games played in September. Any ranking has to propagate information about strength through that graph, and the history of the problem is largely the history of ways to do so: least squares on scoreboard margin [@harvilleUseLinearmodelMethodology1977; @masseyStatisticalModelsApplied1997], paired-comparison models for wins and losses [@bradleyRankAnalysisIncomplete1952; @measePenalizedMaximumLikelihood2003], eigenvector methods [@keenerPerronFrobeniusTheorem1993], and linear-algebraic record-only schemes such as the Colley matrix [@colleyColleysBiasFree2002], one of the computer components of the Bowl Championship Series era [@sternStatisticsCollegeFootball2004; @langvilleWhosNumberOne2012].

These methods disagree partly because they answer different questions. A *predictive* rating asks which team would win a game played next week, and by how much. Margin of victory is informative about that, so a predictive rating should use it, together with any other signal of how well a team played. A *retrodictive* ranking asks what a team has earned by its results. Here margin is usually excluded on purpose, so that a team is neither rewarded for running up a score nor penalised for resting its starters, and a win over a strong opponent is worth more than a win over a weak one. Combining the two into one number, as weighted composites of standardised scores do, gives a quantity that answers neither question and whose weights cannot be validated against anything observable.

This paper keeps the two apart but derives both from one posterior distribution. The contributions are four.

1. A **power model** (@sec-power) for team strength in points on a neutral field, observed through the regulation scoreboard margin and through an efficiency margin built from expected points added per play [@yurkoNflWARReproducibleMethod2019]. The margin is modelled *conditionally* on the efficiency residual, so the two signals share one latent strength without being treated as independent evidence, and their relative weight is estimated rather than set. Strength is pooled within conferences and within three divisional tiers, and carried over from the previous season by an estimated coefficient.
2. A result on how much the efficiency signal adds (@sec-info). Under a Gaussian version of the model the gain in per-game Fisher information about strength has a closed form, and at the fitted parameters it is `r fmt(100 * min(info$gain), 1)`--`r fmt(100 * max(info$gain), 1)`\% --- small, and explained by the estimated scale of efficiency being close to the value at which the gain vanishes.
3. A **resume** measure, Wins Above Benchmark (@sec-resume): for each posterior draw, the number of wins a team has beyond those the draw's twelfth-best FBS team would be expected to earn against the same opponents at the same venues. It is additive over games, never rewards a loss, is centred at zero for a team exactly as strong as the benchmark, and inherits uncertainty in the opponents, the benchmark and the ranks directly from the posterior.
4. A **validation** of the whole system (@sec-computation, @sec-checks, @sec-backtest) on every week of every season from `r first_season` to `r current`: `r n_snap` weekly posteriors fitted by the No-U-Turn sampler, all of which pass convergence gates, posterior predictive checks and prior-sensitivity diagnostics for each season, and a rolling backtest of `r fmt(bt_all$games)` games, each predicted from the posterior fitted through the week before, scored against the result and the closing betting line.

@fig-overview shows how these pieces fit together. @sec-data describes the data, @sec-power and @sec-info the power model, and @sec-resume the resume and the reference rankings. @sec-computation describes fitting and the pipeline, @sec-checks model checking, @sec-backtest the out-of-sample evaluation, @sec-results the `r last_full` season as a worked example, and @sec-discussion the limitations.

::: {#fig-overview fig-scap="Structure of the paper"}

Structure of the paper. One posterior per week feeds both products; the dashed arrow is the only link between them: the Resume values results using opponent and benchmark strengths drawn from the Power posterior, but never uses margin. Each box names the section where it is developed.
:::

**Related work.** The margin model descends from @harvilleUseLinearmodelMethodology1977 and @harvillePredictionsNationalFootball1980, who fit mixed linear models to scoreboard margin with random team effects, and from @sternProbabilityWinningFootball1991, who showed that National Football League margins are close to normal around the betting line with a standard deviation near fourteen points, so that a spread determines a win probability. @glickmanStatespaceModelNational1998 made team strengths evolve over time in a Bayesian state-space model. Using the $t$ distribution for robustness to blowouts follows @langeRobustStatisticalModeling1989. On the retrodictive side, @measePenalizedMaximumLikelihood2003 and @colleyColleysBiasFree2002 give record-only rankings; @sternStatisticsCollegeFootball2004 discusses why the Bowl Championship Series excluded margin from its computer rankings, and @lopezHowOftenDoes2018 quantify how much of a season's outcome is noise, which is the reason a resume should report uncertainty. Wins Above Benchmark is the football analogue of the "wins above bubble" measure used in college basketball selection, with the benchmark placed at the playoff boundary. The workflow follows @gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020.

## Notation {#sec-notation}

@tbl-notation collects the notation. Games are indexed by $g$, teams by $i$ and $j$, conferences by $c$ and divisional tiers by $k \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ for FBS, the Football Championship Subdivision (FCS) and all lower divisions. Posterior draws are indexed by $s = 1, \ldots, S$, and a superscript $(s)$ marks a quantity evaluated at draw $s$. The code keeps its own variable names; @tbl-notation gives both.

```{r}

  "$y_g$", "regulation scoreboard margin, home minus away", "\\texttt{margin}",
  "$e_g$", "efficiency margin: net expected points added", "\\texttt{eff}",
  "$r_i$", "strength of team $i$, points on a neutral field", "\\texttt{r}",
  "$\\eta$", "home-field advantage, points", "\\texttt{hfa}",
  "$\\mu_g$", "$r_{h(g)} - r_{a(g)} + \\eta\\delta_g$, expected margin", "\\texttt{mu}",

  "$\\kappa, \\sigma_m, \\nu$", "loading, scale and degrees of freedom of the margin", "\\texttt{kappa}, \\texttt{sigma\\_m}, \\texttt{nu}",

  "$\\tau_k$", "within-conference spread of tier $k$", "\\texttt{sigma\\_team}",
  "$d_i, \\beta$", "last season's relative rating and its carry-over", "\\texttt{prev\\_dev}, \\texttt{b\\_prev}",
  "$b^{(s)}$", "strength of the benchmark team in draw $s$", "\\texttt{bench}",
```

# Data {#sec-data}

All data come from the CollegeFootballData.com API [@cfbd2026]: every game involving an FBS or FCS team from `r first_season` to `r current`, with line scores, venue, divisional classification and conference of each team; per-game advanced statistics; closing betting lines; and the AP, Coaches and College Football Playoff (CFP) polls. Teams are keyed by the provider's identifiers throughout. Four derived quantities enter the model.

**Regulation margin.** $y_g$ is the home score minus the away score after four quarters, computed from the line scores. A game decided in overtime (`r pct(mean(games$ot, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` of games) therefore contributes a margin of zero. This is deliberate: overtime is a different game, with possession alternating from the opponent's 25-yard line, and its points say little about strength. The win still counts as a win in the resume.

**Efficiency margin.** For each side the provider reports the mean predicted points added (PPA) per play and the number of plays, both with garbage time excluded. PPA is the change in expected points across a play, where expected points are estimated from down, distance and field position [@yurkoNflWARReproducibleMethod2019]. We use the net total,
$$
e_g = \overline{\mathrm{PPA}}_{h(g)} \, n_{h(g)} - \overline{\mathrm{PPA}}_{a(g)} \, n_{a(g)},
$$
which is on the scale of points. It measures how well each offence moved the ball regardless of how drives ended, so it is less exposed than the scoreboard to turnovers returned for touchdowns, missed field goals and fourth-down variance. It is used only when both offences have at least `r cfg$min_plays` non-garbage plays, and is missing otherwise --- in practice for most games against lower-division opponents, which the provider does not chart.

**Tiers and conferences.** Each team is assigned to FBS, FCS or a single pooled tier for Division II, III and NAIA opponents, and to its conference in that season; independents form one pseudo-conference per tier.

**Weeks.** Postseason games are relabelled as one week after the last regular-season week, and a week counts as concluded once at least 90\% of its games are final and six hours have passed since its last kickoff; only a contiguous prefix of weeks can be concluded. A posterior fitted "through week $w$" uses exactly the games of concluded weeks $\le w$.

@tbl-data summarises the data. The 2020 season was shortened and partly cancelled; it is fitted like any other.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "Completed games by season. FBS--FBS games carry most of the information about FBS strength; FBS--FCS games link the two tiers. \\emph{Eff.} is the share of games with an efficiency margin; \\emph{Snap.} is the number of weekly posteriors fitted, including the preseason one from 2015."
g <- games |>
  filter(completed, !is.na(home_points)) |>
  mutate(pair = paste(pmin(home_class, away_class), pmax(home_class, away_class)),
         has_eff = !is.na(home_ppa) & !is.na(away_ppa))
g |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(Games = n(), `FBS--FBS` = sum(pair == "fbs fbs"),
            `FBS--FCS` = sum(pair == "fbs fcs"), `FCS--FCS` = sum(pair == "fcs fcs"),
            Other = Games - `FBS--FBS` - `FBS--FCS` - `FCS--FCS`,
            Eff. = mean(has_eff), Neutral = mean(neutral_site), OT = mean(ot, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  left_join(params |> count(season, name = "Snap."), by = "season") |>
  mutate(across(c(Eff., Neutral, OT), \(x) pct(x)),
         across(c(Games:Other), \(x) fmt(x)),
         season = ifelse(season == current, paste0(season, "$^\\ast$"), season)) |>
  rename(Season = season) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrrrr")
```

# The Power Model {#sec-power}

## Likelihood {#sec-likelihood}

For game $g$ let
$$
\mu_g = r_{h(g)} - r_{a(g)} + \eta\,\delta_g
$$
be the expected regulation margin: the strength difference plus the home-field advantage when the game is not at a neutral site. Both observed signals depend on the teams only through $\mu_g$.

::: {.defn label="Power model likelihood."}
For a game with an efficiency margin,
$$
e_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(\lambda\mu_g,\ \sigma_e^2\bigr), \qquad
y_g \mid e_g, \mu_g \sim t_\nu\bigl(\mu_g + \kappa(e_g - \lambda\mu_g),\ \sigma_m\bigr),
$$ {#eq-lik}
where $t_\nu(m, \sigma)$ is the Student-$t$ distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, location $m$ and scale $\sigma$. For a game without one,
$$
y_g \mid \mu_g \sim t_\nu\bigl(\mu_g,\ \bar\sigma\bigr), \qquad \bar\sigma^2 = \sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2.
$$ {#eq-lik-marg}
Games are conditionally independent given the parameters.
:::

Three features of @eq-lik matter. First, both signals load on the same $\mu_g$, so strength is measured in points of scoreboard margin: $\lambda$ converts it to the efficiency scale, and it is estimated. Second, the margin is modelled *given* the efficiency residual $e_g - \lambda\mu_g$. A team that outplays its expected efficiency usually outscores its expected margin too, and the loading $\kappa$ absorbs that shared component. Were the two modelled as conditionally independent given $\mu_g$, one good performance would be counted twice. Third, the margin is heavy-tailed: the $t$ likelihood lets a 63--0 result inform strength without dominating it [@langeRobustStatisticalModeling1989], and $\nu$ is estimated.

The scale $\bar\sigma$ in @eq-lik-marg is chosen so that the two cases agree in the Gaussian limit.

::: {.thm label="Marginal Margin Lemma."}
Replace the $t_\nu$ law in @eq-lik by the normal law with the same location and scale. Then, marginally over $e_g$, $y_g \mid \mu_g \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_g, \bar\sigma^2)$, and $(e_g, y_g)$ is bivariate normal with mean $(\lambda\mu_g, \mu_g)$ and covariance
$$
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_e^2 & \kappa\sigma_e^2 \\ \kappa\sigma_e^2 & \sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $e_g = \lambda\mu_g + \varepsilon_e$ and $y_g = \mu_g + \kappa\varepsilon_e + \varepsilon_m$ with $\varepsilon_e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_e^2)$ and $\varepsilon_m \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_m^2)$ independent. Then $(e_g, y_g)$ is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, with the stated mean, $\Var(y_g) = \kappa^2\sigma_e^2 + \sigma_m^2$ and $\Cov(e_g, y_g) = \kappa\sigma_e^2$.
:::

Under the $t$ law the marginal of $y_g$ is not exactly $t_\nu(\mu_g, \bar\sigma)$, so @eq-lik-marg is an approximation that matches the location and the scale; it affects only the games without an efficiency margin, which are mostly lopsided games against lower-division teams. The same $\bar\sigma$ and $\nu$ define the predictive win probability.

::: {.defn label="Win probability."}
The probability that team $i$ beats team $j$ at venue $v \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ (away, neutral, home for $i$) is the posterior mean
$$
p_{ij}(v) = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} F_{\nu^{(s)}}\!\left(\frac{r_i^{(s)} - r_j^{(s)} + \eta^{(s)} v}{\bar\sigma^{(s)}}\right),
$$
where $F_\nu$ is the distribution function of the standard $t_\nu$ law. The predicted spread is the posterior mean of $r_i - r_j + \eta v$.
:::

This is the rule of @sternProbabilityWinningFootball1991 with the normal replaced by the fitted $t$ and averaged over the posterior, which widens the predictive distribution by the uncertainty in the ratings.

## Hierarchy and Preseason Information {#sec-hierarchy}

Strength is pooled at two levels: teams within conferences and conferences within tiers.

::: {.defn label="Strength hierarchy."}
For team $i$ in conference $c(i)$ of tier $k(i)$,
$$
r_i = \alpha_{c(i)} + \beta\, d_i + \tau_{k(i)}\, z_i, \qquad
\alpha_c = m_{k(c)} + \omega\, u_c, \qquad
z_i, u_c \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
$$ {#eq-hier}
with $m_1 = 0$. Here $d_i$ is team $i$'s final power rating in the previous season minus the mean final rating of its tier, and $d_i = 0$ when there is no previous rating (the first season, and teams new to the data).
:::

The parameterisation is non-centred [@papaspiliopoulosGeneralFrameworkParametrization2007]: in early weeks each team has one or two games and the data barely constrain $z_i$, which is the regime in which a centred hierarchy produces the funnel geometry that defeats Hamiltonian samplers [@betancourtConceptualIntroductionHamiltonian2017].

The carry-over $\beta$ does the work of a preseason rating. In week 0 no game has been played and the posterior of $r_i$ is centred on $\beta d_i$ plus its conference and tier means; as games accumulate, $\tau_{k}z_i$ takes over. Because $d_i$ is measured against the tier and not the conference, it carries conference strength over as well, so preseason predictions of non-conference games are informative from the first week. Every game is weighted equally within a season: a rolling comparison of recency half-lives of four, six and ten weeks against no down-weighting (`analysis/tune_priors.R`) found no half-life that improved out-of-sample error.

::: {.thm label="Identification."}
The likelihood depends on $\bm r$ only through the differences $r_i - r_j$ between teams in the same connected component of the schedule graph. Under @eq-hier with $m_1 = 0$ the posterior is proper, and the FBS-centred ratings $\tilde r_i = r_i - \bar r_{\text{FBS}}$ are invariant to adding a common constant to every $r_i$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$\mu_g$ is unchanged when the same constant is added to every strength in a connected component. The hierarchy places a proper prior on each $r_i$ given the hyperparameters, and the hyperparameters have proper priors (@tbl-priors), so the joint prior is proper and so is the posterior. The last claim is immediate.
:::

The schedule graph has been connected in every season: FBS--FCS and FCS--lower-division games link the three tiers, and the anchor $m_1 = 0$ is needed only because the prior is centred. Published ratings are the centred $\tilde r_i$, computed draw by draw, so a rating of $+10$ means ten points better than an average FBS team on a neutral field.

@fig-dag draws the full model as a directed acyclic graph.

::: {#fig-dag fig-scap="The power model as a graphical model"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(r"(\begin{tikzpicture}[
  lat/.style={draw, circle, minimum size=0.95cm, inner sep=0pt, font=\small},
  obs/.style={lat, fill=gray!20},
  par/.style={font=\small, inner sep=2pt},
  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=1.8mm]}},
  plate/.style={draw, rounded corners=3pt, inner sep=6pt}]
% hyperparameters
\node[par] (m) at (0,0.2) {$m_k$};
\node[par] (om) at (1.6,0.2) {$\omega$};
\node[par] (tau) at (4.6,0.2) {$\tau_k$};
\node[par] (beta) at (6.4,0.2) {$\beta$};
% conference level
\node[lat] (u) at (0,-1.6) {$u_c$};
\node[lat] (al) at (1.6,-1.6) {$\alpha_c$};
% team level
\node[lat] (z) at (3.0,-3.4) {$z_i$};
\node[obs] (d) at (6.4,-1.8) {$d_i$};
\node[lat] (r) at (4.6,-3.4) {$r_i$};
% game level
\node[lat] (mu) at (4.6,-5.6) {$\mu_g$};
\node[obs] (del) at (2.8,-5.6) {$\delta_g$};
\node[par] (eta) at (1.2,-5.6) {$\eta$};
\node[obs] (e) at (4.6,-7.4) {$e_g$};
\node[obs] (y) at (6.8,-7.4) {$y_g$};
\node[par] (lam) at (2.2,-8.6) {$\lambda, \sigma_e$};
\node[par] (kap) at (9.0,-7.4) {$\kappa, \sigma_m, \nu$};
\draw[arr] (m) -- (al); \draw[arr] (om) -- (al); \draw[arr] (u) -- (al);
\draw[arr] (al) -- (r); \draw[arr] (z) -- (r); \draw[arr] (tau) -- (r);
\draw[arr] (d) -- (r); \draw[arr] (beta) -- (r);
\draw[arr] (r) -- node[right, font=\scriptsize, pos=0.35] {$h(g), a(g)$} (mu);
\draw[arr] (del) -- (mu); \draw[arr] (eta) -- (mu);
\draw[arr] (mu) -- (e); \draw[arr] (mu) -- (y); \draw[arr] (e) -- (y);
\draw[arr] (lam) -- (e); \draw[arr] (kap) -- (y);
\draw[arr] (lam) to[out=-10, in=-120] (y);
\begin{scope}[on background layer]
\node[plate, inner ysep=10pt, fit=(u)(al)] (pc) {};
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=south east] at (pc.south east) {conferences $c$};
\node[plate, inner ysep=10pt, fit=(z)(r)(d)] (pt) {};
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=south east] at (pt.south east) {teams $i$};
\node[plate, inner ysep=10pt, fit=(mu)(del)(e)(y)] (pg) {};
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=south east] at (pg.south east) {games $g$};
\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture})")
```

The power model. Shaded nodes are observed; plates repeat over conferences, teams and games. The efficiency margin $e_g$ is a parent of the scoreboard margin $y_g$, which is how the conditional likelihood of @eq-lik avoids counting one performance twice. The residual enters $y_g$ through $\lambda$ as well, hence the curved edge. When $e_g$ is missing, the edge $e_g \to y_g$ is marginalised as in @eq-lik-marg.
:::

## Priors {#sec-priors}

The structural parameters --- tier offsets, spreads, the carry-over, home field and the likelihood scales --- barely move between seasons, but in the first weeks of a season, with about one game per team, the data cannot estimate them and a vague prior leaves the sampler in a funnel. They are therefore given informative priors, set empirically: each complete season's final posterior (about 1,550 games) was refitted, the posterior means were pooled across seasons, and each prior is centred at the pooled mean with standard deviation at least twice the between-season standard deviation (`analysis/tune_priors.R`). @tbl-priors lists them with the range of posterior means across seasons. The degrees of freedom have the weakly informative $\nu \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(2, 0.1)$ with $\nu > 1$. @sec-supp-justify sets out the empirical basis of each prior, @sec-supp-induced the priors they induce on team strengths, win probabilities and margins, and @sec-supp-perturb refits the model under widened and shifted priors to show that the published end-of-season ratings do not depend on them.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-priors
#| tbl-cap: "Priors (normal, truncated to the support where a parameter is constrained) and posterior means at each complete season's final week. The FBS tier offset is fixed at zero."
labs <- c(
  hfa = "$\\eta$ (home field)", b_prev = "$\\beta$ (carry-over)",
  lambda = "$\\lambda$", kappa = "$\\kappa$", sigma_eff = "$\\sigma_e$", sigma_m = "$\\sigma_m$",
  `mu_tier[2]` = "$m_2$ (FCS)", `mu_tier[3]` = "$m_3$ (lower)", sigma_conf = "$\\omega$",
  `sigma_team[1]` = "$\\tau_1$ (FBS)", `sigma_team[2]` = "$\\tau_2$ (FCS)", `sigma_team[3]` = "$\\tau_3$ (lower)"
)
pri <- tibble::tibble(
  variable = names(labs),
  mean = c(cfg$hfa_mean, cfg$b_prev_mean, cfg$lambda_prior[1], cfg$kappa_prior[1],
           cfg$sigma_eff_prior[1], cfg$sigma_m_prior[1], cfg$tier_mean, cfg$sigma_conf_prior[1],
           cfg$sigma_team_mean),
  sd = c(cfg$hfa_sd, cfg$b_prev_sd, cfg$lambda_prior[2], cfg$kappa_prior[2],
         cfg$sigma_eff_prior[2], cfg$sigma_m_prior[2], cfg$tier_sd, cfg$sigma_conf_prior[2],
         cfg$sigma_team_sd)
)
post <- struct |>
  filter(variable %in% names(labs)) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(lo = min(mean), hi = max(mean), psd = median(sd), .groups = "drop")
pri |>
  left_join(post, by = "variable") |>
  transmute(Parameter = labs[variable],
            Prior = sprintf("$\\mathcal{N}(%s, %s^2)$", fmt(mean, 2), fmt(sd, 2)),
            `Posterior means` = sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(lo, 2), fmt(hi, 2)),
            `Typical post.\\ sd` = fmt(psd, 2)) |>
  ktab(align = "llrr")
```

Using every season to set the priors leaks a little information into the early-week backtest of @sec-backtest: the structural constants for, say, 2016 are informed by later seasons. They are constants of the sport rather than team ratings, and every between-season range in @tbl-priors lies well inside its prior, so we regard the effect as small; it is, however, a departure from a strictly prospective evaluation.

# What the Efficiency Signal Adds {#sec-info}

The efficiency margin is expensive --- it needs play-by-play data --- and a natural question is how much it sharpens the estimate of strength once the scoreboard is known. The Gaussian version of the model answers it in closed form.

::: {.thm label="Information Proposition."}
In the Gaussian model of the Marginal Margin Lemma, the Fisher information about $\mu_g$ carried by one game is
$$
\mathcal{I}_{y} = \frac{1}{\Sigma_{22}} = \frac{1}{\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2}
$$
from the margin alone, and
$$
\mathcal{I}_{e,y} = \frac{\lambda^2}{\sigma_e^2} + \frac{(1 - \kappa\lambda)^2}{\sigma_m^2}
= \mathcal{I}_y + \frac{(\lambda - \lambda^\ast)^2}{\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}},
\qquad \lambda^\ast = \frac{\Sigma_{12}}{\Sigma_{22}} = \frac{\kappa\sigma_e^2}{\sigma_m^2 + \kappa^2\sigma_e^2},
$$ {#eq-info}
from both signals. Hence $\mathcal{I}_{e,y} \ge \mathcal{I}_y$, with equality exactly when $\lambda = \lambda^\ast$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For a Gaussian vector with mean $\bm a\mu$ and known covariance $\Sigma$ the information about $\mu$ is $\bm a^\top\Sigma^{-1}\bm a$. With $\bm a = (\lambda, 1)^\top$, factor the joint density as $p(y)\,p(e \mid y)$: the margin contributes $1/\Sigma_{22}$, and $e \mid y$ is normal with mean $\lambda\mu + (\Sigma_{12}/\Sigma_{22})(y - \mu)$ and variance $\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}^2/\Sigma_{22}$, whose derivative in $\mu$ is $\lambda - \lambda^\ast$. Adding the two informations gives the second form of @eq-info. The first form follows by factoring instead as $p(e)\,p(y \mid e)$: $e$ contributes $\lambda^2/\sigma_e^2$ and $y \mid e$ has mean $(1 - \kappa\lambda)\mu + \kappa e$ and variance $\sigma_m^2$.
:::

The proposition says that the efficiency margin helps exactly insofar as its scale $\lambda$ differs from $\lambda^\ast$, the slope of the regression of $e$ on $y$. If efficiency were nothing but a noisy copy of the scoreboard, its mean would move with $\mu$ exactly as the regression predicts from $y$, and it would add nothing. @tbl-info evaluates @eq-info at the posterior means of each complete season's final fit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-info
#| tbl-cap: "Per-game Fisher information about the expected margin under the Gaussian model, at each season's final posterior means. $R^2$ is the share of the margin's variance explained by the efficiency residual, $\\kappa^2\\sigma_e^2/\\bar\\sigma^2$."
info |>
  transmute(Season = season, `$\\lambda$` = fmt(lambda, 3), `$\\lambda^\\ast$` = fmt(lambda_star, 3),
            `$R^2$` = fmt(r2, 2),
            `$10^3\\mathcal{I}_y$` = fmt(1000 * i_y, 2), `$10^3\\mathcal{I}_{e,y}$` = fmt(1000 * i_joint, 2),
            Gain = pct(gain, 1)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The efficiency residual explains `r pct(min(info$r2))`--`r pct(max(info$r2))` of the margin's variance, so the two signals are strongly related, and the fitted $\lambda$ lies within about `r fmt(max(abs(info$lambda - info$lambda_star)), 2)` of $\lambda^\ast$. The per-game information gain is correspondingly small: `r pct(min(info$gain), 1)` to `r pct(max(info$gain), 1)`, about `r fmt(median(info$gain) * 12, 2)` games' worth over a twelve-game season. Three caveats limit how far this should be read. The calculation is Gaussian, while the fitted $\nu$ ranges from `r fmt(min(info$nu), 0)` to `r fmt(max(info$nu), 0)`; under the $t$ likelihood the efficiency residual also helps decide *which* large margins are outliers, which a Fisher-information calculation at the mean does not capture. It holds $\lambda$, $\kappa$ and the scales fixed, whereas in the fit they are estimated jointly with strength. And it is per game: it does not measure any robustness the efficiency margin brings to the early weeks. The backtest is the arbiter, and a fit without the efficiency likelihood is a direct comparison left for future work (@sec-discussion).

# The Resume {#sec-resume}

## Wins Above Benchmark {#sec-wab}

A resume should value results, not performances, and should value them relative to a standard that matters for selection. The playoff takes twelve teams, so the natural standard is the twelfth-best team.

::: {.defn label="Benchmark."}
In posterior draw $s$, the benchmark strength $b^{(s)}$ is the twelfth largest of the FBS strengths $\{r_i^{(s)} : k(i) = 1\}$.
:::

The benchmark is a strength, not a team: in different draws it is a different team, and its uncertainty is part of the posterior.

::: {.defn label="Wins Above Benchmark."}
Let team $i$ have played games $g \in G_i$, with result $W_g \in \{0, 1\}$ (overtime wins count), opponent $o(g)$ and venue $v_g \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ from $i$'s side. The probability that the benchmark would have won the same fixture is
$$
\pi_g^{(s)} = F_{\nu^{(s)}}\!\left(\frac{b^{(s)} - r_{o(g)}^{(s)} + \eta^{(s)} v_g}{\bar\sigma^{(s)}}\right),
$$
and
$$
\WAB_i^{(s)} = \sum_{g \in G_i}\bigl(W_g - \pi_g^{(s)}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-wab}
The published value is the posterior mean $\WAB_i = S^{-1}\sum_s \WAB_i^{(s)}$ with an 80\% interval.
:::

@eq-wab uses the scoreboard only through $W_g$: margin enters the resume solely by having informed the strengths of the opponents and the benchmark. The following properties are elementary but they are the reason for the choice.

::: {.thm label="WAB Properties."}
For every draw $s$:

(i) *Additivity.* $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ is a sum of per-game contributions $W_g - \pi_g^{(s)}$, each in $(-1, 1)$.
(ii) *Monotonicity.* A win contributes $1 - \pi_g^{(s)} > 0$ and a loss $-\pi_g^{(s)} < 0$; changing any loss to a win raises $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ by exactly one, whatever the opponent.
(iii) *Schedule response.* The contribution of a win is increasing in the opponent's strength and that of a loss is increasing too (a loss to a strong team costs less), and both are decreasing in the venue $v_g$: road wins count for more than home wins.
(iv) *Calibration.* If the model is correct and team $i$ has strength $r_i^{(s)} = b^{(s)}$, then $\E[\WAB_i^{(s)} \mid \text{parameters}] = 0$ for every schedule.
:::

::: {.proof}
Parts (i) and (ii) are immediate from @eq-wab, since $0 < F_\nu < 1$. For (iii), $\pi_g^{(s)}$ is decreasing in $r_{o(g)}$ and increasing in $v_g$ because $F_\nu$ is increasing, and both contributions have the form $\text{const} - \pi_g^{(s)}$. For (iv), under the model $\Pr(W_g = 1) = F_\nu((r_i - r_{o(g)} + \eta v_g)/\bar\sigma) = \pi_g^{(s)}$ when $r_i = b^{(s)}$, so each term has expectation zero.
:::

Property (ii) excludes what the old composite resume did, rewarding a team for *playing* strong opponents regardless of result; (iii) is the precise sense in which the schedule is counted once; and (iv) gives the scale its meaning: a positive $\WAB$ is evidence of having done better than a bubble team would have with the same games. Summing over games makes $\WAB$ a count, not a rate, so a team that plays a thirteenth game can gain from it. That is intended: a conference championship game is a real opportunity to earn or lose standing.

## Strength of Record and Ranks {#sec-sor}

Two further quantities are reported with the resume. The **strength of record** is the probability that the benchmark would do at least as well as team $i$ did, $\SOR_i = \Pr\bigl(\sum_{g \in G_i} B_g \ge \sum_{g \in G_i} W_g\bigr)$ with independent $B_g \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\bar\pi_g)$, $\bar\pi_g$ the posterior mean of $\pi_g^{(s)}$. The sum of independent Bernoulli variables with unequal probabilities is Poisson-binomial, and its distribution is computed exactly by the recursion
$$
P_0^{(0)} = 1, \qquad
P_k^{(t)} = (1 - \bar\pi_t)P_k^{(t-1)} + \bar\pi_t P_{k-1}^{(t-1)}, \quad k = 0, \ldots, t,
$$
over a team's $t = 1, \ldots, |G_i|$ games, in $O(|G_i|^2)$ operations [@hongComputingDistributionFunction2013]. Smaller is more impressive. **Schedule strength** is the benchmark's expected loss rate, $1 - |G_i|^{-1}\sum_g \bar\pi_g$.

Uncertainty in ranks is reported by ranking within each draw.

::: {.defn label="Posterior rank summaries."}
Let $\rho_i^{(s)}$ be the rank of $\WAB_i^{(s)}$ among the teams of $i$'s tier in draw $s$ (1 is best). The published rank orders the posterior means $\WAB_i$; the 80\% rank interval is the 10\% and 90\% quantiles of $\{\rho_i^{(s)}\}_s$; and $\Pr(\text{top } K) = S^{-1}\sum_s \mathbf{1}\{\rho_i^{(s)} \le K\}$ for $K = 1, 4, 12$. The power rank is defined in the same way from $\tilde r_i^{(s)}$.
:::

The published rank orders posterior means rather than taking the median rank, because the median ranks of different teams need not form a permutation.

## Record-only Reference: the Colley Matrix {#sec-colley}

The model's resume uses opponent strengths from a model that sees margins. As a reference that sees only wins and losses we compute the Colley rating [@colleyColleysBiasFree2002; @langvilleWhosNumberOne2012].

::: {.defn label="Colley rating."}
Let $n_i$ be team $i$'s games, $w_i$ and $l_i$ its wins and losses, and $n_{ij}$ the number of games between $i$ and $j$. The Colley ratings $\bm c$ solve $C\bm c = \bm f$ with
$$
C_{ii} = 2 + n_i, \qquad C_{ij} = -n_{ij} \ (i \ne j), \qquad f_i = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}(w_i - l_i).
$$
:::

::: {.thm label="Colley Lemma."}
$C$ is symmetric positive definite, so $\bm c$ exists and is unique, and $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i c_i = \frac{1}{2}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
$C = 2I + L$, where $L$ is the Laplacian of the schedule multigraph, which is positive semidefinite; so $C$ is positive definite. Every column of $L$ sums to zero, so $\bm 1^\top C = 2\bm 1^\top$ and $2\,\bm 1^\top\bm c = \bm 1^\top C\bm c = \bm 1^\top\bm f = n + \frac{1}{2}\sum_i(w_i - l_i) = n$, since every game produces one win and one loss.
:::

The rating is Laplace's rule of succession, $(1 + w_i)/(2 + n_i)$, adjusted for the average rating of the opponents. We compute it on the same games as the posterior and rank within tier.

# Computation and Pipeline {#sec-computation}

## Sampling and Gates {#sec-gates}

Each posterior is sampled with the No-U-Turn sampler [@hoffmanNoUTurnSampler2014] in Stan [@carpenterStanProbabilisticProgramming2017] via CmdStan: `r cfg$chains` chains of `r cfg$iter_warmup` warm-up and `r fmt(cfg$iter_sampling)` sampling iterations, target acceptance `r cfg$adapt_delta`. A fit is accepted only if it passes four gates on every team strength and structural parameter: rank-normalised $\widehat{R} \le `r cfg$gates$rhat`$ and bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least `r cfg$gates$ess` [@vehtariRankNormalizationFoldingLocalization2021], no divergent transitions, and E-BFMI above `r cfg$gates$ebfmi` in every chain [@betancourtConceptualIntroductionHamiltonian2017]. A fit that fails is rerun once with `r fmt(cfg$retry_warmup)` warm-up iterations, target acceptance `r cfg$retry_adapt_delta` and `r fmt(cfg$retry_sampling)` sampling iterations; the posterior for the current week halts the pipeline if it still fails, while a historical week is recorded with a warning. The resume and predictions are computed from `r fmt(cfg$summary_draws)` equally spaced draws.

Of the `r n_snap` weekly posteriors, `r n_pass` pass the gates, `r n_retry` after the retry. @tbl-gates summarises them by season.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gates
#| tbl-cap: "Convergence gates by season, over all weekly posteriors. Worst values are taken over snapshots and over every monitored parameter."
params |>
  group_by(Season = season) |>
  summarise(Snapshots = n(), Passed = sum(passed), Retried = sum(attempts > 1),
            `Max $\\widehat R$` = fmt(max(max_rhat), 3),
            `Min ESS` = fmt(min(pmin(min_ess_bulk, min_ess_tail))),
            Divergent = sum(divergences),
            `Min E-BFMI` = fmt(min(min_ebfmi), 2),
            `Minutes` = fmt(sum(seconds) / 60, 1)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrrr")
```

## The Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

The computation is a `targets` pipeline in R [@landauTargetsPackageDynamic2021; @rcoreteamLanguageEnvironmentStatistical2026], drawn in @fig-pipeline. Its structure enforces the two properties the evaluation depends on. First, the inputs to the week-$w$ posterior contain only games of concluded weeks $\le w$ and are hashed, so a cached posterior is reused exactly when its inputs are unchanged, and new results or betting lines for later weeks never invalidate it. Second, each season's preseason information $d_i$ is the final posterior of the previous season, a dependency the pipeline tracks, so refitting one season refits every later one.

::: {#fig-pipeline fig-scap="The targets pipeline"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(r"(\begin{tikzpicture}[
  box/.style={draw, rounded corners=2pt, align=center, font=\small,
              inner sep=4pt, minimum height=0.9cm, fill=white},
  store/.style={box, fill=gray!12},
  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]}, thick},
  node distance=0.45cm and 0.55cm]
\node[store, text width=2.1cm] (api) {CFBD API};
\node[store, text width=2.1cm, right=of api] (json) {JSON cache\\\scriptsize one file per call};
\node[store, text width=2.1cm, right=of json] (db) {DuckDB\\\scriptsize games, stats, lines, polls};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, below=1.1cm of db] (data) {\texttt{data\_}$s$\\\scriptsize one season};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of data] (weeks) {\texttt{weeks\_}$s$\\\scriptsize concluded weeks};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of weeks] (inputs) {\texttt{inputs\_}$s$[$w$]\\\scriptsize games $\le w$, $\bm d$};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, below=1.1cm of inputs] (snaps) {\texttt{snaps\_}$s$[$w$]\\\scriptsize NUTS, gates, summaries};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, left=of snaps] (checks) {\texttt{checks\_}$s$\\\scriptsize PPC, priorsense, LOO};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, right=of snaps] (prior) {final ratings of $s$\\\scriptsize $\to$ $\bm d$ for $s{+}1$};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, below=1.1cm of snaps] (all) {\texttt{snapshots}, \texttt{ratings}\\\scriptsize + polls};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, right=of all] (bt) {\texttt{backtest}\\\scriptsize week $w$ predicts $w{+}1$};
\node[box, text width=2.4cm, right=of bt] (out) {dashboard, reports, this paper};
\draw[arr] (api) -- (json); \draw[arr] (json) -- (db); \draw[arr] (db) -- (data);
\draw[arr] (data) -- (weeks); \draw[arr] (weeks) -- (inputs);
\draw[arr] (inputs) -- (snaps); \draw[arr] (inputs) -- (checks);
\draw[arr] (snaps) -- (all); \draw[arr] (all) -- (bt); \draw[arr] (bt) -- (out);
\draw[arr] (snaps) -- (prior);
\draw[arr, dashed] (prior.north) to[out=90, in=-20] (inputs.south east);
\draw[arr] (checks) |- (all);
\node[font=\scriptsize, anchor=south] at (inputs.north) {map over weeks $w$};
\end{tikzpicture})")
```

The computation as a `targets` pipeline. Grey boxes are external stores; white boxes are targets, with $[w]$ marking a dynamic branch per concluded week and $s$ a season. The dashed edge is the only cross-season dependency: season $s$'s final ratings become season $s+1$'s preseason information. The checks feed the diagnostics report. A weekly update calls the API about six times and refits only the new week.
:::

# Model Checking {#sec-checks}

Each season's latest posterior is refitted with the pointwise log-likelihood stored, and three checks are run on it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gabryVisualizationBayesianWorkflow2019]. This section summarises them across seasons; @sec-supp examines two posteriors in full detail --- sampler diagnostics, convergence, posterior geometry, prior-to-posterior learning, predictive distributions and influence.

## Posterior Predictive Checks {#sec-ppc}

Replicated regulation margins are drawn from @eq-lik-marg, rounded to whole points so that they can land exactly on the thresholds of the statistics, and compared with four observed statistics: the standard deviation of the margin, the share of games within seven points, the share decided by 28 or more, and the home team's win rate in true home games. @fig-ppc shows the result for every season.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ppc
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive checks at each season's latest posterior. Bars: central 90\\% interval of the statistic over 400 replicated seasons; points: the observed value, filled when it falls outside the interval. Three statistics are reproduced; the share of one-score games is not."
#| fig-scap: "Posterior predictive checks by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.55
ppc <- map_dfr(checks, \(x) mutate(x$ppc, season = x$season))
ppc |>
  mutate(outside = observed < rep_lo | observed > rep_hi,
         statistic = factor(statistic, levels = unique(statistic))) |>
  ggplot(aes(season)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = rep_lo, ymax = rep_hi), colour = col_ref, linewidth = 2.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed, shape = outside), colour = col_ink, size = 1.6, fill = col_ink) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 21, `TRUE` = 19), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~statistic, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(first_season, current, 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
within7 <- ppc |> filter(statistic == "Share within 7 pts")
```

The model reproduces the spread of margins, the frequency of blowouts and home-field advantage, but in `r sum(within7$observed > within7$rep_hi)` of `r nrow(within7)` seasons the observed share of games decided by seven points or fewer (`r fmt(min(within7$observed), 2)`--`r fmt(max(within7$observed), 2)`) lies above the replicated interval. Real margins bunch around one score more than a Student-$t$ around the rating difference allows: late-game behaviour (running out the clock when ahead, playing for a tying field goal when behind), key numbers, and the regulation ties that overtime games contribute all push mass towards zero. The misfit is in the *shape* of the margin distribution near zero; the win probabilities, which depend on the location and the tails, are well calibrated (@sec-backtest).

## Prior Sensitivity {#sec-sens}

Power-scaling sensitivity [@kallioinenDetectingDiagnosingPrior2024] perturbs the prior and the likelihood by raising each to a power near one, estimates the resulting change in each marginal posterior by importance sampling, and flags a parameter whose posterior moves under both (prior--data conflict) or under neither (weak likelihood). @tbl-sens counts the flags across seasons.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sens
#| tbl-cap: "Power-scaling sensitivity by parameter, at each season's latest posterior. Sensitivities are the cumulative Jensen--Shannon distance between the base and the power-scaled posteriors; the conventional threshold is 0.05."
sens <- map_dfr(checks, \(x) mutate(x$sensitivity, season = x$season)) |>
  filter(!is.na(variable))
sens |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(prior = median(prior), likelihood = median(likelihood),
            conflict = sum(grepl("conflict", diagnosis)),
            weak = sum(grepl("weak", diagnosis)), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(variable = coalesce(unname(labs[variable]), "$\\nu$")) |>
  transmute(Parameter = variable, `Prior (median)` = fmt(prior, 3),
            `Likelihood (median)` = fmt(likelihood, 3),
            `Seasons flagged: conflict` = paste0(conflict, "/", n),
            `weak likelihood` = paste0(weak, "/", n)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrr")
```

No parameter is flagged for a weak likelihood in more than one season, and $\lambda$, $\kappa$, $\sigma_e$ and the FBS and FCS spreads are clean in almost every season; home field $\eta$ and $\sigma_m$ show a mild conflict in about a third of seasons. The flags concentrate on four parameters, all as prior--data conflicts: the lower-division offset $m_3$ and spread $\tau_3$, identified each season by a few dozen lopsided games; the FCS offset $m_2$; and the degrees of freedom $\nu$, whose Gamma prior is weakly informative but whose likelihood is flat once $\nu$ exceeds about 15, where the $t$ and normal laws are hard to tell apart. The first three priors were set from the pooled seasons on purpose (@sec-priors), and a conflict in any one season reflects that season's departure from the pooled mean; none of the three enters an FBS rating except through the handful of cross-tier games. The sensitivity of $\nu$ matters more for the tails of the predictive distribution than for any rating.

## Leave-one-out Cross-validation {#sec-loo}

Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [@vehtariPracticalBayesianModel2017; @vehtariParetoSmoothedImportance2024] estimates the expected log predictive density of a new game, with the Pareto $\hat k$ diagnostic flagging games whose removal would change the posterior too much for the approximation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo
#| tbl-cap: "PSIS-LOO at each season's latest posterior. $p_{\\mathrm{loo}}$ is the effective number of parameters; the last column counts games with $\\hat k > 0.7$."
map_dfr(checks, \(x) mutate(x$loo, season = x$season, week = x$week)) |>
  left_join(params |> select(season, week, n_games), by = c("season", "week")) |>
  left_join(ratings |> count(season, week, name = "teams"), by = c("season", "week")) |>
  transmute(Season = season, Games = fmt(n_games), Teams = teams,
            `$\\widehat{\\mathrm{elpd}}_{\\mathrm{loo}}$` = fmt(elpd_loo, 0), SE = fmt(se, 0),
            `$p_{\\mathrm{loo}}$` = fmt(p_loo, 0), `$\\hat k > 0.7$` = n_bad_k) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The effective number of parameters is close to, and below, the number of teams plus the handful of structural parameters, as expected of a hierarchical model that shrinks the least-informed teams towards their conference. A few games per season have high $\hat k$; they are almost always the only link between a lower-division team and the rest of the graph, whose strength is then determined by that single game.

# Out-of-sample Evaluation {#sec-backtest}

## Design {#sec-bt-design}

Every game of week $w+1$ is predicted from the posterior fitted through week $w$, which by construction (@sec-pipeline) contains no information from week $w+1$ or later. This is a rolling-origin evaluation [@tashmanOutofsampleTestsForecasting2000] with one origin per week, and it covers every week of every season from `r first_season + 1`, when a preseason posterior first exists, including week 1 predicted from the preseason. Predictions are scored by the absolute error of the spread, the Brier score [@brierVerificationForecastsExpressed1950] and the log loss of the home win probability, both strictly proper [@gneitingStrictlyProperScoring2007], and against the closing betting line where one exists. A betting line is the sharpest public forecast available, since it aggregates information --- injuries, weather, motivation --- that no ratings model sees [@levittWhyAreGambling2004]. Beating it is not the aim; coming close to it with public results alone is evidence that the ratings are sound.

## Accuracy {#sec-bt-accuracy}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-backtest
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling out-of-sample accuracy. MAE is the mean absolute error of the predicted margin, in points; \\emph{Line} is the closing betting line on the same games; ATS is the share of games in which the model's side of the line covered, pushes excluded."
ov |>
  transmute(Games = scope, N = fmt(games), `MAE` = fmt(mae_model_lined, 2),
            `MAE, line` = fmt(mae_vegas, 2), RMSE = fmt(rmse, 2),
            Brier = fmt(brier, 3), `Log loss` = fmt(logloss, 3),
            Accuracy = pct(accuracy, 1), ATS = pct(ats_win_rate, 1)) |>
  ktab(align = "lrrrrrrrr")
```

Over all `r fmt(bt_all$games)` predicted games the mean absolute error is `r fmt(bt_all$mae, 1)` points and the favourite wins `r pct(bt_all$accuracy, 1)` of the time. On FBS--FBS games, which all have a line, the model's error is `r fmt(bt_fbs$mae_model_lined, 2)` points against the line's `r fmt(bt_fbs$mae_vegas, 2)`: the market is better by about `r fmt(bt_fbs$mae_model_lined - bt_fbs$mae_vegas, 1)` points per game, and the model picks the side that covers in `r pct(bt_fbs$ats_win_rate, 1)` of games, indistinguishable from the 50\% expected of a forecast with no edge on the market. @fig-bt-week shows how accuracy evolves through the season. The error is largest in week 1, predicted from the preseason alone, falls quickly, and is flat from about week 4; the gap to the line is roughly constant. The Brier score *rises* through the season, not because predictions get worse but because conference play and the postseason pair more evenly matched teams, which are intrinsically harder to call.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bt-week
#| fig-cap: "Rolling out-of-sample accuracy on FBS--FBS games by the week predicted. Left: mean absolute error of the model's spread and of the closing line on the same games. Right: Brier score of the model's win probability. Weeks after the last regular-season week are the postseason and have few games."
#| fig-scap: "Out-of-sample accuracy by week"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.42
bw <- bt$by_week
p1 <- bw |>
  select(week, games, Model = mae_model_lined, `Closing line` = mae_vegas) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Model, `Closing line`)) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(aes(size = games), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model = col_power, `Closing line` = col_ref)) +
  labs(x = "Week predicted", y = "Mean absolute error (points)")
p2 <- bw |>
  ggplot(aes(week, brier)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_power, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(size = games), colour = col_power, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Week predicted", y = "Brier score")
p1 + p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Calibration {#sec-calibration}

A win probability is useful to the resume only if it is calibrated, because $\WAB$ subtracts $\pi_g$ from an observed result. @fig-calibration groups all predicted games by their win probability and compares the mean prediction in each group with the observed frequency.

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of out-of-sample home win probabilities, all games. Games are grouped into deciles of predicted probability; each point is a group's mean prediction and observed home win rate, with a 95\\% binomial interval. The diagonal is perfect calibration."
#| fig-scap: "Calibration of out-of-sample win probabilities"
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-asp: 0.9
#| out-width: "65%"
cal <- bt$calibration |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(obs * (1 - obs) / n), lo = pmax(obs - 1.96 * se, 0), hi = pmin(obs + 1.96 * se, 1))
max_cal_gap <- max(abs(cal$obs - cal$pred))
cal |>
  ggplot(aes(pred, obs)) +
  geom_abline(colour = col_faint, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = col_power, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = col_power, size = 1.8) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Predicted home win probability", y = "Observed home win rate")
```

Every decile lies within `r fmt(100 * max_cal_gap, 1)` percentage points of the diagonal. The resume's benchmark probabilities are computed with the same predictive distribution, so this is also direct evidence that the $\pi_g$ in @eq-wab are on the right scale.

@fig-bt-season repeats the comparison with the line season by season. The gap is stable, which suggests it reflects information the market has and the model does not rather than a drifting model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bt-season
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample mean absolute error by season on FBS--FBS games, model and closing line on the same games. The last season is in progress."
#| fig-scap: "Out-of-sample error by season"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.36
bt$by_season |>
  select(season, Model = mae_model_lined, `Closing line` = mae_vegas) |>
  pivot_longer(-season) |>
  ggplot(aes(season, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Model = col_power, `Closing line` = col_ref)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seasons) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "MAE (points)")
```

# The `r last_full` Season {#sec-results}

This section uses the final posterior of the `r last_full` season, after the postseason, to show what the two products look like and how they relate. @tbl-top lists the top of the resume.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-top
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Final ", last_full, " FBS resume. $\\WAB$ with its 80\\% interval; the resume rank with its 80\\% rank interval; the power rating in points above an average FBS team with its rank; and the Colley and final AP ranks for reference.")'
top <- fin_last |> arrange(resume_rank) |> slice_head(n = 25)
top |>
  transmute(` ` = resume_rank, Team = gsub("&", "\\&", team, fixed = TRUE), Record = paste0(wins, "--", losses),
            `$\\WAB$` = sprintf("%s \\,{\\scriptsize(%s, %s)}", fmt(wab, 2), fmt(wab_lo, 1), fmt(wab_hi, 1)),
            `Rank 80\\%` = paste0(resume_rank_lo, "--", resume_rank_hi),
            `$\\Pr(\\le 12)$` = fmt(resume_p12, 2),
            Power = sprintf("%s (%d)", fmt(power, 1), power_rank),
            Colley = colley_rank, AP = ifelse(is.na(ap_rank), "--", ap_rank)) |>
  ktab(align = "rllrrrrrr")
```

The rank intervals are the point of reporting a posterior. @fig-intervals shows them for the top 25 in both products. Resume ranks are sharper than power ranks at the top, because once the results are fixed only the valuation of the opponents is uncertain; power ranks, which describe strength itself, overlap heavily beyond the first few teams.

```{r}
#| label: fig-intervals
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Posterior rank intervals at the end of ", last_full, " for the top 25 of the resume. Points are the published ranks; bars the central 80\\% of the rank across posterior draws. Teams are ordered by resume rank.")'
#| fig-scap: "Posterior rank intervals, resume and power"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.75
top |>
  transmute(team = factor(team, levels = rev(team)),
            Resume_r = resume_rank, Resume_lo = resume_rank_lo, Resume_hi = resume_rank_hi,
            Power_r = power_rank, Power_lo = power_rank_lo, Power_hi = power_rank_hi) |>
  pivot_longer(-team, names_to = c("product", ".value"), names_sep = "_") |>
  mutate(product = factor(product, levels = c("Resume", "Power"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = team, colour = product)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.55,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = r), size = 1.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Resume = col_resume, Power = col_power)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40)) +
  labs(x = "Rank (1 = best)", y = NULL)
```

@fig-scatter plots the two products against each other for every FBS team. The relation is monotone but loose: teams above the curve have won more than their strength would predict, and teams below it have lost close games or played a schedule that gave them few chances.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Resume against power at the end of ", last_full, ", all FBS teams. The dashed line is zero Wins Above Benchmark: teams above it did better than the twelfth-best team would have with their schedule. Labelled: the resume top 12.")'
#| fig-scap: "Resume against power"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.62
fin_last |>
  mutate(lab = ifelse(resume_rank <= 12, team, NA)) |>
  ggplot(aes(power, wab)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_ref) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = col_faint, linewidth = 0.6, span = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = resume_rank <= 12), size = 1.3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.6, colour = col_ink, na.rm = TRUE,
                           min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1, max.overlaps = 30) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = col_resume, `FALSE` = col_ref), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Power rating (points vs. average FBS team, neutral field)", y = "Wins Above Benchmark")
```

@fig-trajectory follows the power rating of the resume top six through the season. Preseason ratings come from the carry-over alone and are wide; by mid-season the intervals have roughly halved.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Weekly power rating in ", last_full, " for the final resume top six, with 80\\% posterior intervals. Week 0 is the preseason posterior; the last point is the final posterior after the postseason.")'
#| fig-scap: "Weekly power rating trajectories"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.55
six <- top$team[1:6]
ratings |>
  filter(season == last_full, tier == 1, team %in% six) |>
  mutate(team = factor(team, levels = six)) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, power)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = power_lo, ymax = power_hi), fill = col_power, alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = col_power, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~team, nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Power rating (points)")
```

Finally, @fig-agreement measures agreement between the products and the references by Spearman rank correlation among FBS teams, week by week, averaged over the complete seasons. The resume tracks the record-only Colley ranking closely from the first weeks --- both are functions of the record --- and diverges from it only in how opponents are valued; the power rating is less correlated with both, as it should be, because it uses margin and efficiency. Agreement with the AP poll, which ranks only 25 teams, is computed on those 25.

```{r}
#| label: fig-agreement
#| fig-cap: "Spearman rank correlation between rankings of FBS teams, by week, averaged over complete seasons. Correlations with the AP poll use the teams it ranks."
#| fig-scap: "Agreement between rankings"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-asp: 0.45
cr <- function(a, b) {
  ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
  if (sum(ok) < 5) NA_real_ else suppressWarnings(cor(a[ok], b[ok], method = "spearman"))
}
agree <- ratings |>
  filter(tier == 1, week > 0, season %in% complete) |>
  group_by(season, week) |>
  summarise(`Resume vs. Colley` = cr(resume_rank, colley_rank),
            `Power vs. Colley` = cr(power_rank, colley_rank),
            `Resume vs. Power` = cr(resume_rank, power_rank),
            `Resume vs. AP` = cr(resume_rank, ap_rank),
            `Power vs. AP` = cr(power_rank, ap_rank), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-c(season, week)) |>
  group_by(week, name) |>
  summarise(rho = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(is.finite(rho))
agree |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("Resume vs. Colley", "Resume vs. AP", "Resume vs. Power",
                                        "Power vs. Colley", "Power vs. AP"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, rho, colour = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Resume vs. Colley` = col_resume, `Resume vs. AP` = col_resume,
                                 `Resume vs. Power` = col_ink,
                                 `Power vs. Colley` = col_power, `Power vs. AP` = col_power)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`Resume vs. Colley` = "solid", `Resume vs. AP` = "dashed",
                                   `Resume vs. Power` = "dotted",
                                   `Power vs. Colley` = "solid", `Power vs. AP` = "dashed")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Spearman correlation")
```

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The design principle of this paper is that a ranking should say which question it answers, and that different questions can share a model without sharing a formula. The power rating and the resume come from one posterior and are never mixed: the resume borrows the model's estimate of how hard each game was, and nothing else. That separation has a cost --- two numbers where the public expects one --- but each number can then be checked against something observable, the power rating against future games and the resume against the calibration that property (iv) of the WAB Properties requires.

**Limitations.** Several choices deserve more work.

1. *The margin distribution near zero.* The model underpredicts one-score games in every season (@sec-ppc). This affects spread and cover probabilities rather than win probabilities, but a likelihood that bunches margins --- a two-component mixture, a margin-dependent scale, or a discrete model on the score itself --- should be compared by LOO.
2. *Strength is constant within a season.* A team that loses its quarterback in October is rated as the average of its season. A random walk $r_{i,w} = r_{i,w-1} + \tau\epsilon_{i,w}$, as in @glickmanStatespaceModelNational1998, would estimate how quickly ratings should move rather than fixing it; the half-life experiments of @sec-hierarchy found no benefit from down-weighting old games, which suggests $\tau$ is small but not that it is zero.
3. *The value of the efficiency margin.* The Information Proposition suggests the efficiency likelihood adds little per game under a Gaussian approximation. A backtest of the model with that likelihood removed would settle whether it earns its data cost.
4. *Priors from the whole history.* The structural priors use every complete season (@sec-priors), so early-week backtest results for past seasons are slightly optimistic. A strictly prospective version would set each season's priors from earlier seasons only.
5. *No offence--defence split.* The model rates teams by margin, so it gives spreads but not totals or projected scores; splitting $r_i$ into offensive and defensive strengths, validated against the betting total, is the natural extension.
6. *Games are exchangeable.* Motivation, rest, travel, injuries and weather are all absent; the gap to the closing line in @sec-backtest is a measure of how much they matter.

<!--
Supplementary posterior checks. Draws come from the `supplement` target
(R/06_supplement.R), which refits two posteriors with every draw kept; the
